title: Implicit 4D Gaussian Splatting for Fast Motion with Large Inter-Frame Displacements
one_liner: SPIN-4DGS reconstructs fast-moving dynamic scenes by predicting Gaussian attributes from explicit space-time positions instead of forcing one shared Gaussian description to fit several far-apart frames.
lead: Dynamic 4D Gaussian splatting works well when motion between frames is small. It breaks when objects move far between frames. Existing methods either deform a canonical set of Gaussians over time or optimize explicit 4D Gaussian attributes that are shared across frames. Under large displacement, both strategies can lose the moving object: the canonical space may never allocate enough Gaussians to it, or the shared attributes may collapse toward the easier static background. SPIN-4DGS changes the representation. It first gathers explicit spatiotemporal positions for Gaussians and then predicts the other Gaussian attributes from those positions with a small feed-forward network. That separates where the Gaussian is from how it should look at that time.

problem.h2: Why fast motion breaks existing 4D Gaussian splatting
paras: A dynamic scene renderer must place many small Gaussian primitives in 3D space and assign each one a size, orientation, color, and opacity. When motion between frames is small, a Gaussian can often be tracked or deformed smoothly over time. When motion is large, that assumption becomes fragile. A ball may jump far across the image, or a limb may move far enough that a shared canonical description no longer covers it.

The paper identifies two failure modes. In deformable approaches, the canonical space may omit fast-moving content at initialization, so later deformation has nothing to move. In explicit 4D approaches, one set of Gaussian attributes is optimized across several timestamps, and updates for easy background regions can dominate the loss. The moving object then becomes blurred or disappears.

callout.b: The breakdown is mostly in attribute learning.
callout.html: Positions may still roughly track the motion, but color, opacity, scale, and rotation collapse because background fitting dominates the optimization.

steps.text: Slice and refine Gaussian positions across time so the point set covers the whole motion trajectory.
Prepare each position as an input to a compact implicit predictor.
Use a 4D hash encoder to turn each space-time location into features suitable for attribute prediction.
Predict scale, rotation, color, and opacity with multi-branch decoders.
Render the scene and update the predictor so the reconstructed frames match the observed images.

paras: SPIN-4DGS changes how time is built into dynamic Gaussians. Instead of learning time-varying attributes directly as explicit per-Gaussian variables or as deformations from one canonical state, it learns a mapping from explicit space-time positions to attributes.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: attribute stability under large displacement
hidden.name: Whether moving-object Gaussians keep coherent attributes over time
paras: The critical quantity is not just position error. It is attribute stability: can the representation keep the right appearance and support of a fast-moving object as it appears in very different places at nearby times? If color or opacity collapses, the object vanishes from the rendered result even if some positions remain.

The paper argues that explicit space-time positions make this stability easier to learn. Once each timestamp has its own position sample, the predictor can assign attributes conditioned on that sample alone instead of forcing one shared attribute state to serve conflicting frames.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark parts of the representation that must remain coherent for moving objects to stay visible.

reads.html: The hard part is keeping the moving object alive in the representation. SPIN-4DGS tracks that by making appearance depend on explicit space-time positions.
The method decouples position estimation from attribute prediction, so cross-frame interference is reduced and fast-moving Gaussians keep more stable color, opacity, and shape.

mechanism.h2: Why explicit space-time positions reduce collapse
paras: In an explicit 4D model with shared attributes, one update can improve one frame while hurting another, because several timestamps are tied together through the same Gaussian state. That creates cross-frame interference. Background regions usually dominate the reconstruction loss, so the optimization tends to favor them. Fast-moving objects lose out because they occupy fewer pixels and appear in more variable positions.

SPIN-4DGS reduces that coupling by conditioning attribute prediction on explicit coordinates in space and time. Each point on the motion path gets its own query. The predictor can therefore emit different color, opacity, scale, or rotation values at different timestamps without storing separate explicit variables for every point. That keeps memory manageable while still separating far-apart states of the same object.

The learned implicit predictor also shares information across many Gaussians. That matters because similar local motion patterns can reuse the same decoder rather than learning isolated per-point values. The representation is therefore compact in storage but flexible in time, which is exactly what fast motion needs.

stages.s: Collect and refine explicit space-time positions
Encode positions with a 4D hash representation
Decode Gaussian attributes from each query point
Render and optimize with reconstruction loss
Sharper dynamic reconstruction under large displacement

math.words: A small network takes a space-time coordinate and outputs the Gaussian attributes needed for rendering at that location and time.
math.equation: attributes(x, y, z, t) = f_theta(x, y, z, t)
symbols: the spatial position and timestamp of a Gaussian query

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a basketball appears at position P1 at time t1 and at a far-away position P2 at time t2.
A shared explicit attribute model tries to use one Gaussian description across both times, so updates from background-heavy frames can wash out the ball.
SPIN-4DGS instead queries f_theta at (P1, t1) and at (P2, t2).
The two queries can return different opacity and color values while still sharing the same predictor.
That separation matters because the renderer no longer needs one attribute state to explain two far-apart appearances.

math.note: The point of the mapping is practical. It isolates large-displacement states while keeping the representation compact.

charts.title: Prior 4DGS baselines on fast sports scenes
charts.note: Fast objects blur or vanish when cross-frame interference and canonical misses accumulate.

charts.title: SPIN-4DGS
charts.note: The paper reports a +1.83 PSNR gain over D3DGS on the Basketball scene, along with stronger SSIM on the same benchmark, because explicit space-time queries reduce cross-frame interference on the fast-moving ball.

items.html: If the spatiotemporal position set misses part of the motion path, attribute prediction cannot recover it later, because the decoder only answers the queries it is given.
If the feed-forward network cannot model the needed time-varying appearance, the method may keep positions but still produce dull or unstable attributes.

items.b: Fast motion plus occlusion remains hard.
items.html: Large displacement is only one source of difficulty. Heavy occlusion or missing views can still make the rendered evidence insufficient for accurate reconstruction.
The method is strongest when the initial space-time positions cover the full trajectory and the decoder has enough capacity to map those positions to stable attributes across time.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Use a short multi-view sports clip with a small fast-moving object. Compare a baseline 4D Gaussian renderer against SPIN-4DGS. Visualize the sampled space-time positions, the rendered frames, and a crop around the moving object over time. The demo should emphasize whether the object stays present and sharp after many training steps.
demo.closing: The demo succeeds when explicit space-time queries preserve moving-object visibility better than a shared-attribute baseline under large frame-to-frame motion, because the renderer no longer forces one attribute state to explain several far-apart timestamps.
